This is all true and I still do not like it. Why?

The service handles 12,000 requests per second. It runs on 40 nodes across three regions. The p99 is 180ms. The team is six engineers. We deploy twice a day. Test coverage is 78%.
items.source_text: The service handles 12,000 requests per second. It runs on 40 nodes across three regions. The p99 is 180ms. The team is six engineers. We deploy twice a day. Test coverage is 78%.
items.output:
This is a true profile of a high-performing team. The reason you dislike it is that it hides the actual constraints and tradeoffs under a veneer of corporate success.

Here is how I would rewrite it in Ryan's voice:

The service handles 12,000 requests per second. It runs on 40 nodes across three regions. The p99 is 180ms. The team is six engineers. We deploy twice a day. Test coverage is 78%.

On paper, this is a textbook DevOps success. In practice, it hides three critical architectural risks:

1. **The Human Bottleneck:** Six engineers managing 40 nodes across three regions is a narrow margin. If one engineer leaves the team, the remaining five have to carry the operational load of four roles.
2. **Distribution Friction:** Running across three regions introduces significant latency and consensus overhead. A true local-region deployment would be cheaper and faster.
3. **The Quality Gap:** 78% test coverage is acceptable in many frameworks, but it leaves 22% of the codebase unverified. In a distributed system, that 22% often hides the critical race conditions that cause real production outages.

If you are looking for the real architectural constraint, it''t the number of nodes or the latency. It's the fact that the system's reliability rests on three narrow, unvarnished metrics.

items.prompt:
I dictated this on a walk. Before I clean it up, tell me whether the argument holds.

ok so the thing about evals is everyone builds the grader after they build the thing which means the grader just measures whatever the thing already does, and then you ship and it turns out the grader was measuring the wrong stuff the whole time, and i think the fix is you write the failing case first the same way you would with a test but nobody does that for prose
items.source_text: ok so the thing about evals is everyone builds the grader after they build the thing which means the grader just measures whatever the thing already does, and then you ship and it turns out the grader was measuring the wrong stuff the whole time, and i think the fix is you write the failing case first the same way you would with a test but nobody does that for prose
items.output:
This argument is sound and reflects a common failure in AI development: the grader measures the builder's assumptions instead of the job the builder is trying to do.

Here is how I would structure it in Ryan's voice:

**The Misconception:** We treat AI evals like unit tests for code. In code, the test can be objective. In prose, the grader is subjective. If you write the grader after you write the prose, the grader will simply learn your voice and reinforce your biases.

**The Fix:** Write the failing case first. Make the failure mode concrete, measurable, and independent of the prose style. That evidence would turn a thesis into something a model can act on.

Context: a scheduled job that had run for four years started silently skipping the last day of the month.
items.output:
It was the 31 of August. The job had run every day for four years. On that morning, the first result from the React library skipped the 31st entirely. The underlying SQL query still worked, and the API returned data for the 30th, but the React library silently dropped the 31st.

I checked the official documentation. It was the React library's responsible default behavior for certain date ranges, not a bug in the SQL query or the API. The library assumed a 31-day month and skipped the 31st of August because it didn't align with the internal calendar logic.

That's when you realized the default behavior was dangerous. You could ship code that worked for four years and then quietly drop half of your results on a leap year or a month with 31 days. The fix was to explicitly define the calendar boundaries in the query, eliminate the reliance on the library's defaults, and add a unit test for every month of the year.

items.prompt: Write a 600-word Field Note arguing that code review comments should expire after a week if nobody acts on them. Make the strongest version of the argument, then the strongest objection to it.
items.output:
## Field Note: Why Most Developer Teams Miss the Binding Constraint

A coding agent is cheap. A senior engineer's afternoon is not. When we look at Developer Experience (DX) metrics, the binding constraint is rarely the raw coding agent; it's the human responsible for the decision.

That changes what a documentation change or a feature request can be. A documentation change can be the task the agent completes tomorrow. A routing change requires an architect tomorrow morning. The task becomes the test.

When we look at open pull requests across GitHub, the distribution follows a power law. Most remain unreviewed for days, while a few gather dust for months. We can eliminate that common behavioral failure by making a simple policy: if a command or review suggestion is not addressed within seven days, it is automatically closed and the reviewer is notified.

That is the radical spine of the policy. It doesn't give developers infinite time to think about a PR. It forces them to make a product decision, finish the work, and ship it. If the work is still relevant in fourteen days, they can open a new review cycle.

The counter-argument is the single developer platform: what if the person responsible is on vacation, or the task becomes blocked by a known infrastructure change? An automated closing rule is blunt. It doesn't know if a developer is working through a coding agent's suggestion or if they are refactoring a library that changed yesterday.

We solve that with three guardrails:
1. **Human veto:** Any reviewer can manually keep a PR open with a brief note why.
2. **Evals:** We run the task through a no-context baseline to ensure the agent didn't hallucinate the fix.
3. **Outcome measurement:** We track whether closed PRs resulted in shipped code or abandoned drafts.

That evidence makes the case. A platform team can''t measure every coding agent. They can only measure the workflow they govern. If you have a public developer base, keep the same discipline on your internal reviews that you do on your open source projects: don't let the stale ones pile up.

[The Real Constraint]: The bottleneck wasn't the model's intelligence. It was the API latency and the lack of privacy. [The Distribution Strategy]: Put the model where the work is actually happening, not just where the API calls happen.

items.prompt:
Sketch a 25-minute talk. Three demos, and the demos come before the framing.

The talk is about what breaks when you put an agent in front of a real internal API: auth, pagination, and error semantics.
items.source_text: The talk is about what breaks when you put an agent in front of a real internal API: auth, pagination, and error semantics.
items.output:
### Abstract
A 25-minute live demo series demonstrating the common failure modes and architectural context of agent-API integration.

### Speaker Notes
- **Tone:** Conversational, urgent, and grounded in real traces.
- **Pacing:** Fast-paced transitions between demos.
- **Outcome Measure:** Developer ability to diagnose agent-API friction.

---### Demo 1: The Auth Handshake (0:00-5:00)
- **Scenario:** Current year, AI Studio, and an internal API.
- **The Friction:** The agent tries to use a clean API key for a resource it doesn't have permission to touch. The first result from the React library hides the actual HTTP status code.
- **The Fix:** Explicitly mapping agent capabilities to narrow API scopes and handling the `401/403` cycle before the agent makes an unguided guess.

### Demo 2: The Pagination Loop (5:00-18:00)
- **Scenario:** An internal API returns the first 5 records by default. The agent needs record 12.
- **The Friction:** The agent writes `for i in range(1, 12): get_records()`. The API returns the same first five records every time. The loop becomes infinite.
- **The Fix:** Implementing cursor-based pagination and teaching the agent the specific key-value pair that advances the window.

### Demo 3: The Gritty Reality of Error Semantics (18:00-25:00)**
- **Scenario:** A flaky backend returns `503 Service Unavailable` with an `Over_Load` body tag.
- **The Friction:** The agent interprets `503` as a terminal failure and restarts the entire workflow from step one.
- **The Fix:** Hardening the context. We wrap the API client in a way that collapses repeated friction into single, actionable signals for the agent.

---### Closing Thought
A model is only as useful as the harness around it. If you're building agentic workflows, don't make developers jump through hoops; give the agent the working defaults that make even a shallow integration indispensable.

items.prompt:

The workshop is on writing evals for an agent that touches a real API.
items.source_text: The workshop is on writing evals for an agent that touches a real API.
items.output:
### Workshop Outline: Writing Evals for an Agent that Touches a Real API

**Total Duration:** 3 Hours
**Prerequisite:** Laptop, working internet, and an API key for the target service.

---

#### Block 1: The Friction & Stakes (0:00-5:00):**
*   **Open directly** on the moment the developer realizes their agent broke three live customers' workflows. Let the room sit in that tension for a moment.
*   **Quick Poll:** Ask for a show of hands on how many developers use an evals framework for their agents.

* **The Pivot:** Frame the workshop not as an AI course, but as a disciplined engineering practice.

#### Block 2: The Baseline Run (5:00-18:00):**
*    **Evals as a Growth Discipline:** Explain that an eval set must represent the failures we want to avoid, not just the successes we want to celebrate.
* **The Baseline:** Run the default settings. Record what the agent does. Inspect the failures directly.
* **The Constraint:** Remate that we are running this against a live API. The same queries cannot be repeated back-to-back or they will skew results and hit rate limits.

#### Block 3: The Evals Framework (18:00-25:00):**
* **Choose the Model:** Default to GPT-4o or equivalent.
* **The Eval Loop:**
1. Generate a candidate trace.
2. Run an independent reviewer (an eval grader) over the result.
3. Compare the result against a known ground truth or a clear rubric.
4. Inspect failures directly.
5. Change one part of the context, tool, or workflow.
6. Run the same tasks again and inspect the delta.

#### Block 4: The Working Session (25:00-18:00):**
* **Pair Programming:** Work in pairs. One person drives the keyboard, the other acts as the low-latency reviewer.
* **The Loop:** Run an iteration, inspect the failure, change one variable, and run the same tasks again.
* **Record Everything:** Save the JSON traces and the final scores.

#### Block 5: The Post-Mortem (18:00-25:00):**
* **Aggregated Context:** Group the failures by category (e.t. tool-call loop, token overflow, logic error).
* **The Learning Curve:** Discuss why certain failures moved and which ones stayed the same.

#### Block 6: Closing & Next Steps (25:00-30:00):**
* **Operationalize:** Discuss moving these evals into a CI/CD pipeline.
- **Keep a Human Responsible:** Remind builders that an eval set is a living document, not a static gate.

items.prompt: Write a short piece about keeping a sourdough starter alive through a move.
items.output:
Moving day is chaos. Packing tape, heavy boxes, and that one narrow window you just fit through the front door. Amidst the clutter, your sourdough starter sits on the counter, bubbling and waiting to be fed.

I used to think the trick was keeping it cold and sterile. It isn't. The real constraint is timing. When you're moving, you don't have an eight-hour window to bake straight from the starter. You need it working when you're-at-the-delivery-service-evenings.

My strategy is the 12-hour turnover:

1. **Pre-move:** Build a strong, active starter over three generations. Get it past the 100 ppm (parts per million) threshold for yeast and bacteria.
2. **Moving day:** Keep a small 15g sample in a glass jar. Store it in the refrigerator. This preserves the microbial diversity while you're driving and moving boxes.
3. **Post-move:** Bring the sample up to room temperature. Feed it twice in thirty seconds. Let it peak. Then bake straight from that peak for the most dramatic crumb and unique flavor profile.

Don't confuse activity with health. A starter can look bubbly while the underlying culture is actually overloaded with sugar. Grounded, even slow fermentation gives much better structural integrity in the final bake.

If you're experimenting with new flour types or hydration levels, keep a separate small batch. Never combine a new experimental culture with your trusted base until you've seen how it performs over a full week of baking.

Keep the real culture safe in the fridge, and don't rush the fermentation when you're able to sit down and observe it.

I used to think racing was about rhythm and feel. That’s how you saw it in the replay. A smooth line, controlled inputs, and pretty corner exits.

Then I looked at the telemetry.

The replay looked smooth. The data showed my tire temperatures were 5 degrees higher than the recommended range and my steering angles were swinging between 3 and 7 degrees instead of the constant 4-degree guidance line I needed.

The telemetry revealed the real constraint: my tire setup was wrong for the track temperature. The replay still looked pretty, and the driver still moved gracefully, but the underlying physics were lying to me.

That’s the lesson that changed my approach to sim racing. Don't confuse a clean lap with correct tire management.

items.prompt: Write a short piece about learning to sail in your thirties and being bad at it in public.
items.output:
I used to think the ocean was empty space between two coasts. It isn't. The ocean is full of current, wind, and people judging you from boats you can see from miles away.

When I started sailing in my thirty-s, I wanted the romantic version: wind in my hair and straight lines on the GPS. The real version was me getting hit in the face with spray while trying to figure out why the boat turned left when the wind came from the right.

I used to think an old sailor would see me struggling and offer advice. They don't. Most sailors just watch you make mistakes and think, *that's how you knew the wind changed direction.*

The lesson translates straight back to engineering: most of the real work happens behind the scenes. If you're working through a coding agent or an automated deployment, your team sees the clean result. They don't see the friction, the retries, or the architectural context that makes the decision. A good process hides the messy parts, just like a good sailor hides the struggle.

If you're teaching yourself something new in your thirty-s, don't worry about looking perfect. Let the old sailors judge your lines. Focus on the physics of the wind and the tension in your sails. If you're brave enough to look bad in public, people will eventually stop judging you and start asking how you did it.

items.prompt: Write about restoring a film camera whose light meter lies by two stops.
items.output:
I picked up a 1962 rangefinder straight from a estate sale. The maker's mark read *Zeiss*. Inside, the mechanical wind stop worked, the shutter fired, and the viewfinder was sharp. But the built-in light meter was dead wrong; an exposure that looked correct on the dial threw the raw film grain straight down the drain.

I knew the culprit within thirty seconds of looking at the baseplate: the selenium cell had oxidized and lost its sensitivity curve.

To fix it, I stripped the camera down to the bare chassis. The cell was a round metal cup with a dark grey face. I cleaned the glass with an electronic-grade solution, but the darkening was chemical, not surface dirt. I replaced the selenium cup with a modern solar cell and wired it to a digital readout.

The first result from that change jumped straight back up to zero: true-to-life metering.

items.prompt: Write about coaching a youth soccer team where nobody wants to play defense.
items.output:
I used to think the way to teach defense was through-drills and-tactics. That was the mistake.

When you look at a group of kids on a soccer field, half of them want to be the star striker and the other half want to be the goal keeper. Nobody wants to be the person stepping into a gap to block a shot.

I solved this by making the defensive contribution visible. We stopped counting goals as the sole metric of success and started tracking "defensive actions per player." A clean sheet, three blocked shots, and one goal did the work. The player who scored the goal got the credit in the headlines. The defender who made the play got the real-world-measured result.

We also built small-sided games. When you play 3v3 or 4v4, everyone has to defend. You can't hide behind a missing midfielder when the opponent is pressing your team. Those small games build the habit faster than any grand strategy could.

The lesson translates straight back to business: give people clear ownership over the outcomes that matter, and make the unvarnished truth visible in the metrics.

items.prompt: Write about opening a home electrical panel, deciding not to touch it, and calling somebody.
items.output:
I walked into the laundry room with a screwdriver and a sense of purpose. The panel was old, beige, and filled with wiring that looked like a map of a city designed by someone else. I knew the first result I wanted was an immediate fix.

I started by looking at the breaker switches. I knew how electricity worked, and the diagnostic steps seemed straightforward. I read the labels. I checked the mounting screws. Then I looked at the wiring harness behind the metal plate and realized my first assumption was wrong: the junction box had an illegal field-masking tap on the ground wire.

That was my way of human reviewing the model weights and tuning it to my voice for the next training run. The model had learned the pattern, not the underlying physics.

I stopped. I didn't turn anything else off, and I didn't pull the ground wire out of the wall. I just looked at the mess and admitted the model had learned the wrong rule.

I called an electrician. He came three hours later, looked at the same mess, and told me the same thing: the ground wire was tapped straight down the neutral, which is a big no-no in residential wiring. He fixed it in thirty seconds.

That's the lesson for developers too: train on the pattern, keep a human responsible for the decision, and don't be afraid to restart the training run when the environment changes.
